title: Processes and CPU scheduling
subtitle: A process is a program in motion. The scheduler decides whose turn it is — and every policy is a different answer to “fair to whom?”.

sections.title: A program that is running
sections.body:
A program on disk is inert text. A process is that program in execution: its code, the values in its registers, a stack, a heap and a program counter that says where it is. Ten processes can run the same program at once and still be ten different processes, because each carries its own state.

A process is always in one of a handful of states. It is ready when it could run but the CPU is busy, running while it holds the CPU, and waiting when it needs something — a disk block, a key press — before it can continue. The operating system keeps the ready processes in a queue and the scheduler picks the next one. Everything in this chapter is about that pick.

questions.prompt: A process asks the disk for a block and has to wait. Which state does it move to?

choices.text: Ready — it is still eager to run.
Waiting (blocked) — it cannot use the CPU until the I/O completes.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: Ready means “could run right now”. A process blocked on a disk read cannot, so putting it in the ready queue would just waste a turn on the CPU.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: A blocked process is alive and will continue once its data arrives. Termination is only for a process that has finished or been killed.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It gives up the CPU voluntarily because it has nothing useful to run, and the scheduler must not pick it until the event it awaits has happened. Only then does it become ready again — never straight back to running.

sections.title: What “good scheduling” means
sections.body:
“Fast” is not one number. Four times are computed for every process, with arrival (AT) the moment it joins the ready queue and burst (BT) the CPU time it needs:

  • Completion time (CT) — the clock reading when it finishes.
  • Turnaround time (TAT) = CT − AT — everything the user waited, running included.
  • Waiting time (WT) = TAT − BT — time spent in the ready queue doing nothing.
  • Response time (RT) = first CPU − AT — how long before anything happens at all.

Schedulers trade these against each other. Average waiting time is the usual yardstick for batch work; response time is what an interactive user feels.

worked.why: Three processes arrive together: P1 needs 24, P2 needs 3, P3 needs 3. Under first-come-first-served they run in arrival order, so P1 finishes at 24, P2 at 27 and P3 at 30.
Turnaround is completion minus arrival. All arrive at 0, so it equals the completion time.
Average waiting time is the mean of those three: (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 17. Check this against Figure 2.3.1 — the card reports the same number.

sections.title: First come, first served — and the convoy
sections.body:
FCFS is the simplest policy: run the process that arrived first, to completion. It is easy to implement (a plain queue) and completely fair in the sense of order — but its average waiting time depends violently on who arrives first. A long job at the head of the queue makes every short job wait behind it: the convoy effect.

Press ▶ and watch the Gantt chart fill. Then the same three jobs under SJF (shortest job first), which always picks the smallest burst among those waiting.

questions.prompt: The same three jobs arrive in a different order: P2, P3, P1 (short ones first). What happens to FCFS’s average waiting time?

choices.text: It drops sharply — to 3, the same as SJF here.
It stays exactly the same, because the jobs are the same.
It gets worse, because short jobs now run before the long one.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: FCFS has no idea how long jobs are; it only sees the order. Put the short jobs at the front and they finish almost at once, so only the long job waits (for 0, 3 and 6 units → an average of 3). The policy did not get smarter — the input got kinder.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The set of jobs is the same but the waiting times are not: waiting is time spent behind others, and who is behind whom changed. Average waiting time under FCFS is a property of the arrival order.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: Running short jobs first is precisely what removes waiting: a long job delays everything after it, a short one barely delays anything.

verify.caption: Verify — FCFS with the short jobs first
verify.note: Same jobs, kind order: run it and compare with Figure 2.3.1.

figures.caption: Figure 2.3.1 — FCFS on 24 / 3 / 3
figures.note: FCFS: P1 (24) runs first, so P2 and P3 wait 24 and 27 units.

figures.caption: Figure 2.3.2 — SJF on the same jobs
figures.note: SJF: the two short jobs go first; average waiting collapses.

sections.title: Round Robin: everyone gets a turn
sections.body:
Interactive systems cannot let one job hog the CPU. Round Robin gives each process a fixed time quantum; when the quantum expires the process goes to the back of the ready queue and the next one runs. New arrivals join the queue behind the ones already waiting — but ahead of the process that has just been pre-empted.

The quantum is the one knob. Very large: Round Robin degenerates into FCFS. Very small: the CPU spends its time switching (saving and restoring state) rather than working. Compare the three cards below on the same jobs.

questions.prompt: A designer makes the quantum smaller and smaller. What is the cost?

choices.text: Nothing — a smaller quantum is strictly fairer.
More context switches — CPU time is burnt on switching instead of on the jobs.
The scheduler runs out of memory for the queue.

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: It is fairer, but fairness is not free: the switch overhead is the price, and past a point it dominates.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Every switch saves one process's registers and loads another's. With q = 1 the three jobs above cause 9 switches; with q = 100 only 2. Each switch is pure overhead, so a tiny quantum buys responsiveness with throughput.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: The ready queue holds the same number of processes at any quantum; what grows is the number of times the CPU changes hands.

figures.caption: Figure 2.4.1 — quantum 1
figures.note: q = 1: fair to the extreme, but 9 context switches.

q4.order: P1 P2 P3 P1 P1 P1 P1 P1

figures.caption: Figure 2.4.3 — quantum 100
figures.note: q = 100: longer than every burst, so it is FCFS again.

sections.after: With quantum 4 the jobs above finish with an average waiting time of 5.67 — worse than SJF's 3, better than FCFS's 17, and every process got the CPU within a few units. That last property, not the average, is why time-sharing systems use it.

sections.title: Shortest remaining time, priority and aging
sections.body:
SJF is provably optimal for average waiting time, but it needs the future: nobody knows a burst length in advance (real systems estimate it from history). Its pre-emptive form, SRT (shortest remaining time), re-decides every time a process arrives: if the newcomer needs less than what the running job has left, it takes the CPU.

Priority scheduling runs the most important job first; the trap is starvation — a low-priority job that never gets a turn while urgent ones keep arriving. The cure is aging: raise a job's priority the longer it waits. HRRN (highest response ratio next) builds that idea into a formula, (W + B) / B, which grows as a job waits.

questions.prompt: In a priority scheduler a low-priority process has waited for hours. Which mechanism prevents it waiting forever?

choices.text: Aging — its priority rises the longer it waits.
Running the job twice as long when it does get the CPU.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Starvation is a property of the policy, not of the process: as long as higher-priority jobs keep arriving, the low one is never chosen. Slowly raising the priority of waiting jobs guarantees that eventually it is the best in the queue.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: The quantum decides how long a job runs once chosen; starvation is about never being chosen at all.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: That would only make each rare turn longer — the job would still wait indefinitely for the first one.

figures.caption: Figure 2.5.1 — SRT on four arriving jobs
figures.note: SRT: watch P1 being pre-empted when P2 arrives. Average waiting 6.5, versus 7.75 for non-pre-emptive SJF.

sections.title: Threads and the Linux scheduler
sections.body:
A thread is a strand of execution inside a process: threads share the code, heap and open files, but each has its own stack and registers. Creating and switching threads is cheaper than processes because far less state has to change. Modern kernels schedule threads, not whole processes.

Linux's Completely Fair Scheduler drops fixed quanta altogether. Each runnable task accumulates virtual runtime — CPU time scaled by its weight (nice value) — and the scheduler always runs the task with the smallest virtual runtime, kept in a red-black tree so the leftmost node is found in O(log n). A task that has had little CPU is behind, so it is chosen; the ideal is every task advancing at the same virtual rate.

figures.caption: Figure 2.6.1 — the Completely Fair Scheduler as a loop
figures.note: The loop CFS repeats. A task that ran a lot has a large vruntime and moves right; one that waited moves left.

problems.prompt: Processes P1(0,8), P2(1,4), P3(2,9), P4(3,5) — (arrival, burst). Find the average waiting time under SRT and under non-pre-emptive SJF.
problems.answer: Run both in the cards above. SRT gives 6.5 and non-pre-emptive SJF gives 7.75. Pre-emption lets the short P2 (4) take over from P1 the moment it arrives, so the short jobs finish sooner and total waiting falls. The price is more context switches and needing to know the remaining time.

verify.note: The SRT schedule that produces the figure.

problems.prompt: Three processes all arrive at t = 0 with bursts 24, 3 and 3. Find the average waiting time under Round Robin with quantum 4.
problems.answer: Order of service: P1 (4), P2 (3, done at 7), P3 (3, done at 10), then P1 runs the rest of its 24 alone. Waiting: P1 = 30 − 24 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7 → average 5.67 (Figure 2.4.2). The two short jobs no longer wait behind the long one — that is the point of time-slicing.

problems.prompt: A process arrives at 2, needs 5 units, and completes at 20. Give its turnaround and waiting time.
problems.answer: TAT = CT − AT = 20 − 2 = 18. WT = TAT − BT = 18 − 5 = 13. The process spent 13 units in the ready queue and 5 running.
